2-xm.what: Sessions for Sérgio Mendes (Homecooking) and The Brothers Johnson (Look Out for #1)
2-xm.text: Lewis played a home-built bank of four SEMs from a digital keyboard, one of the ways SEMs were used for polyphony before Oberheim’s own Four Voice. Each 2-XM module is one of these SEMs.

2-xm.what: The Life Aquatic with Steve Zissou (score)
2-xm.text: Mothersbaugh used his Two Voice for the score’s electronic sounds and cues.

2-xm.what: Drokk: Music Inspired by Mega-City One
2-xm.text: Made largely on three original Two Voice units, for music first meant for the film Dredd.
Between them the composers owned three or four Two Voice units, which Salisbury says made many of the score’s heavy, noise-driven sounds.

2-xm.on: Roland Jupiter-8 (the lead), with an Oberheim, a Sequential Pro-One and a Roland SH-2
2-xm.text: The theme’s arpeggio is played on an Oberheim Two Voice, by hand rather than by a sequencer.
Salisbury has said the four-note synth theme heard in the film’s trailer was played on a Two Voice and then processed.

b2600.text: Edgar Winter played the lead lines on an ARP 2600, with its keyboard hung from a strap so he could move around the stage.
The sleeve credits Arp and Moog synthesizers together. Wonder was an early 2600 owner and had the panel of his own unit labelled in Braille.

b2600.on: ARP 2600 and ARP Pro Soloist, with a Moog
b2600.text: Patrick Gleeson and Hancock are both credited on the 2600 and the Pro Soloist, and Hancock on a Moog as well. Gleeson had joined the band as Hancock’s synthesizer technician.

b2600.on: ARP 2600 and ARP Odyssey, with an EMS Synthi A and a Synthanorma sequencer
b2600.text: Two side-long pieces, “Bayreuth Return” and “Wahnfried 1883”. Schulze’s first solo album to use a sequencer.
Zawinul played two 2600s, one with its keyboard scaled upside down so that familiar fingerings gave unfamiliar lines.
One of a handful of synths on the album, used alongside an EMS VCS3 and an organ for its washes of filtered noise and effects.
Joe Zawinul’s ARP 2600 is one of the main voices on the album, played with a lot of hand-moved pitch bending.

b2600.what: Star Wars — the voice of R2-D2
b2600.text: The sound designer built the robot’s chirps and whistles on an ARP 2600, blended with his own voice.

b2600.on: ARP 2600, run by Michel Geiss’s Matrisequencer
b2600.text: The 2600 is one of the main voices on the album, with sequenced lines from the Matrisequencer that Michel Geiss built.
The band have used a 2600 from the early records to the late ones; Martin Gore was photographed playing one during the Sounds of the Universe sessions.
Hannett owned a 2600 and its sequencer and used them on the second album. The synthesizers on Unknown Pleasures the year before were a Transcendent 2000 and an ARP Omni, not this one.
The 2600 is the instrument Clarke is most associated with. He has owned several and has kept using them across four decades of records.
Producer Daniel Miller made the kick and snare sounds on a 2600 with a sequencer in place of a drum machine: a pitch-swept sine for the kick, filtered noise for the snare.

b2600.on: ARP 2600 (percussion blasts), with a 5U modular and a Polymoog
b2600.text: Made after the directors asked for a monster theme. Stein sequenced it on the eight-step Encore Event Generator in his large 5U modular, with rising dissonant pads from a Polymoog, sub-bass and percussion blasts from an ARP 2600.

buchla-easel.text: Not an Easel record: it was made on the Buchla 100 series modular, the system the Easel’s circuits grew out of.
Not an Easel record: played on a Buchla 200 modular, the series whose circuits the Music Easel puts in one case.
The whole Forse series was played on one Music Easel, which Cortini had spent several years looking for.
Made with the new Music Easel Smith bought in 2013, as was Euclid the following year.
Improvised pieces made entirely on Cohen’s 1970s Music Easel, recorded in Berlin in 2014: quick, scattered tones and patterns.
Smith built the rippling, sequenced patterns of her early albums on a Music Easel.

buchla-easel.on: Buchla Music Easel, with woodwind and Smith’s voice
buchla-easel.text: Smith wrote the album on the Easel, then arranged woodwind parts and added her voice. The Easel plays most of what you hear.
Smith’s Music Easel, played against Ciani’s 200e in long, slowly changing improvisations.

buchla-easel.on: Buchla Music Easel, with an EMS Synthi 100 and other synths
buchla-easel.text: The Music Easel remains the main voice, joined on some tracks by the rare EMS Synthi 100.

buchla-easel.on: Buchla Music Easel with an Epoch Modular Benjolin
buchla-easel.text: A 50-minute improvisation on the Easel and a Benjolin, recorded in one take with no edits.

cat.text: Devo are named among the best-known CAT users on the Vintage Synth Explorer and Cherry Audio lists, and Mark Mothersbaugh has been filmed playing one. No single Devo record credits it by name.
Daly has said his first synth was a CAT mono synth bought for £30, which he sold for £40 to buy a Moog Prodigy. That was before China Crisis made their first records, so the CAT is not on them.
The CAT is the synth most often linked to the song’s keyboard break, played by Eddie Rayner. The band’s keyboards at the time also included a Prophet-5 and a Yamaha CS-80.
Tom Rowlands has talked in interview about using a CAT in the studio. No single track is credited to it.

Tom Jenkinson has said the drum track of "Bubble Life" was built layer by layer from CAT sounds played by hand on its keyboard, and that apart from a Roland SH-101 it was the only vintage synth he owned. The CAT is on the left of the album cover.
Segall is seen playing a CAT in a short clip made for Adult Swim’s Squidbillies. Which records it is on is not known.
A CAT can be seen in a photo of Simon Green’s studio that he posted online. Which records it is on is not known.

deepmind-12d.text: The bubbling riff is the Jupiter-8’s arpeggiator, run with a sequencer and a TR-808 drum machine. The backing track was built in a day.

Nick Rhodes played a C major seventh chord into the Jupiter-4’s arpeggiator set to random, which gives the scattered synth line. The noise at the very start is a piano with metal rods thrown on its strings, played backwards.

Johannes Schmoelling played the hypnotic line on the Jupiter-8’s arpeggiator rather than a sequencer, set to random instead of up or down. Two Jupiter-8s were synced together, panned apart and sent through a delay timed to the pattern.
The bouncing keyboard part and the solo that sounds like a steel drum are both a Juno-60. The solo is said to have been recorded in one take.
Jonathan Cain has said the opening synth riff is a Jupiter-8.

deepmind-12d.on: Roland Juno-60, doubled by a Moog Memorymoog
deepmind-12d.text: Co-writer Rob Hyman built the song on a Juno-60 pad with its own stereo chorus switched on. He has said he still remembers the memory number, 61.
The theme from Beverly Hills Cop. The sawtooth lead is a Jupiter-8; the bass is a Moog modular and the drums a LinnDrum.
George Michael played the synth parts himself on a Juno-60, with a bass guitar and sleigh bells alongside.

deepmind-12d.on: Roland Juno-60, layered with a Yamaha DX7
deepmind-12d.text: The riff is a Juno-60 layered with a DX7.
A slow ballad George Michael played almost entirely himself, with soft synth chords under the voice.

Bass and melody both come from a Juno-60, with a TR-909 for the drums. Larry Heard recorded it by bouncing between two cassette decks, days after buying the two machines. It is one of the founding records of deep house.

From the album Watermark. The piece began as a melody Enya improvised on the Juno-60’s arpeggiator. She said in 1989 that the Juno was one of their favourites: they had meant to replace its parts with better sounds but could not find any.

deepmind-12d.on: Roland Juno-106 chords, sampled into a Casio FZ-1 and layered with a Roland D-50
deepmind-12d.text: The warm pad is Juno-106 chords with the chorus on and the filter well down, sampled and layered with the D-50’s “Warm Strings” preset.
Another early hit built on the same hoover sound, released the same year as "Mentasm".

deepmind-12d.who: Second Phase (Joey Beltram and Mundo Muzique)
deepmind-12d.text: The lead is the Alpha Juno 2 factory sound "What the…", sampled and edited further. The sound became known as the hoover and was copied across rave, jungle and hardcore.

deepmind-12d.on: Roland Juno-106 through a Boss Heavy Metal distortion pedal
deepmind-12d.text: Their MIDI technician Matt Cox has said the Juno-106 through a Boss Heavy Metal pedal is the signature sound of “Chemical Beats”, and that they still played it that way live.

deepmind-12d.on: Roland Juno-106, with a Jupiter-6 and a Yamaha TX81Z
deepmind-12d.text: An ambient album made in a spare bedroom in Somerset. Mark Pritchard has said the Juno-106 played bass and some of the pads, which they pitch-shifted with a Zoom unit, and that the signature reverb was an Alesis Quadraverb on a chorus-reverb setting: noisy and detuned.

deepmind-12d.on: Roland Juno-106 (chords), with a Roland TR-909
deepmind-12d.text: The chord sequence is a Juno-106, which Rick Smith has called “a supreme piece of kit”. The drums are a 909, heavily driven through the mixing desk.
Xavier de Rosnay has said the Juno-106 plays the opening arpeggio and the chorus chords of “D.A.N.C.E.” and the bass on “Genesis”.

deepmind-12d.on: Roland Jupiter-8 (the lead), with an Oberheim, a Sequential Pro-One and a Roland SH-2
deepmind-12d.text: The theme to the Netflix series is built from many synthesizers. The slow, haunting lead is a Jupiter-8 that the two composers fitted with MIDI themselves. The arpeggio was played by hand on an Oberheim, the heartbeat pulses on a Pro-One and the bass on an SH-2.

ems-vcs3.on: Lowrey organ through an EMS VCS3
ems-vcs3.text: Pete Townshend’s organ part was fed through a VCS3, whose filter and envelope turn it into the pulsing, rhythmic pattern the song opens with.

ems-vcs3.on: Two EMS VCS3s, one borrowed from WDR radio in Cologne, with organ
ems-vcs3.text: The band’s first use of a synthesizer. Christopher Franke and a guest, Roland Paulyck, each played a VCS3 after learning it in a day and a half.
Brian Eno played a VCS3 in Roxy Music, using it to treat the band’s instruments and add electronic squeals and chatter.
Hawkwind’s electronics players, Dik Mik and Del Dettmar, used VCS3s for the swooping, whooshing sounds that run through the band’s records of this period.
Brian Eno is credited with “VCS3 synthesizer, treatments”: the noises and effects that sit around the band.

ems-vcs3.on: EMS VCS3 (the solo), with a Synthi AKS
ems-vcs3.text: Richard Wright’s VCS3 solo was fed through a long tape delay, which gives the rising and falling line before the guitar comes in.
The racing eight-note line comes from the Synthi AKS’s sequencer, not a VCS3, though the voice is the same family.

ems-vcs3.on: EMS synthesizer (the model is not credited), with a Moog
ems-vcs3.text: Tim Blake’s EMS synth builds a bed of delayed, bubbling tones for the first half of the track before the band joins in.

ems-vcs3.on: EMS VCS3, with an ARP Solina and a Minimoog
ems-vcs3.text: In the long opening section Richard Wright layers VCS3, Solina and Minimoog sounds over the drone. Sound On Sound names the VCS3 but not the passage it plays.
The mechanical throb that opens the track is credited to a VCS3.
Jarre used his EMS synthesizers for the wind, sea and sweeping effects on the album.

ems-vcs3.on: EMS Synthi AKS, also used to filter Robert Fripp’s guitar
ems-vcs3.text: Brian Eno’s Synthi AKS, the VCS3 in a briefcase: an oscillator set very slow and the noise filter worked by hand give the chattering texture that builds through the song.

ems-vcs3.on: EMS VCS3, through an Electro-Harmonix Small Stone phaser
ems-vcs3.text: The VCS3 gives the sweeping echo effects, and with an Eminent organ through the phaser makes the string pads.

James Murphy has said the swooping chords are the Synthi A: he set the joystick to move the oscillator pitches between chords and faded a fixed lower note in and out by hand with the third oscillator’s level.
Cortini made music for his grandfather’s Super 8 films of his childhood using only a Synthi AKS, with no overdubs, and kept the mistakes in as the films kept theirs.

grandmother.on: Moog Grandmother, with a Moog Matriarch and a Prophet
grandmother.text: Tygner played the album’s synth parts by hand and ran them through a Vermona RetroVerb for spring reverb and a little drive. Which tracks use the Grandmother is not stated.

jupiter-4.on: Roland Jupiter-4 (arpeggio and chords), ARP Odyssey (melody), Yamaha CS-80
jupiter-4.text: Peter Howell’s arrangement for the 1980 series: the Jupiter-4’s arpeggio leaps across octaves and its chords are doubled on a CS-80, while an ARP Odyssey plays the tune.

jupiter-4.on: Roland System-700, Prophet-5, Oberheim OB-X and Roland Jupiter-4, with a Polymoog and a Micromoog
jupiter-4.text: The credits list synths for Richard Barbieri, Steve Jansen and David Sylvian. Barbieri has described the set-up as in transition, using whatever came to hand, including a hired Polymoog; the System-700 was his own, bought in 1978.

jupiter-4.on: Roland Jupiter-4, alongside a Minimoog, a Polymoog and a Prophet-5
jupiter-4.text: The album credits list a Jupiter-4 among the newer polysynths Numan added to his Moog-based sound on Telekon. Which tracks it plays on is not documented.

jupiter-4.on: Roland Jupiter-4 and Kawai 100F (Vince Clarke), Yamaha CS-5 (Martin Gore), Moog Prodigy (Andy Fletcher)
jupiter-4.text: The credits name each member’s synth, with Daniel Miller programming an ARP 2600 and a Roland MC-4 sequencer. The riff is usually credited to Clarke’s Jupiter-4.

jupiter-4.on: Roland Jupiter-4 and System-700, sequenced from a Roland MC-8, with a Linn LM-1 drum machine
jupiter-4.text: The producer Martin Rushent built each song up from a Linn LM-1 pattern, with sequenced synth parts locked to it; the System-700, MC-8 and Linn were his own. The main synth riff of “Don’t You Want Me” is credited to the Jupiter-4.

jupiter-4.on: Roland Jupiter-4, with a Micromoog bass
jupiter-4.text: Dolby has said the shimmering arpeggio that runs through the song is the Jupiter-4. The bass is a Micromoog.
Nick Rhodes used a Jupiter-4 on Duran Duran’s first records; the running arpeggio of “Rio” is often credited to its arpeggiator.
Most of the keyboard parts, including the horns in the chorus and the strings, recorded on four tracks two octaves apart, are the Jupiter-4.
The Jupiter-4 plays the arpeggios that run across the song’s nine minutes.
The song is named after the synth that plays its dark drone and slow pulses. Van Etten demoed most of the album on a Jupiter-4.

jupiter-6.on: Roland Jupiter-6 (bass line and chords), with a Roland TR-707
jupiter-6.text: The Jupiter-6 plays both the arpeggiated bass line and the wavering chords over a TR-707 beat: one of the first Chicago house records.

jupiter-6.on: Roland Jupiter-6, Yamaha DX7 and E-mu Emulator II, joined by MIDI (the bass)
jupiter-6.text: For Stephen Hague’s re-recording, the bass part was played on three instruments linked by MIDI: a Jupiter-6, which gives it its body, a DX7 and an Emulator II. The choirs, strings and the trumpet solo are Emulator samples.

jupiter-6.on: Roland Jupiter-6, with a Roland TR-707
jupiter-6.text: Larry Heard has said he made “Washing Machine” and “Mystery of Love” on the same day he brought the Jupiter-6 and TR-707 home, in 1984. It was released on Trax in 1986.
The loud, distorted bass line is a Jupiter-6 that Moby bought second-hand from a New York shop, and later learned had been Joey Beltram’s.
The bubbling sound that comes in before the vocals is a broken Jupiter-6. Paul Hartnoll has said it started making sounds it had never made before, and they recorded them.

jupiter-6.on: Roland Juno-106, with a Jupiter-6 and a Yamaha TX81Z
jupiter-6.text: An ambient album made in a spare bedroom in Somerset. Mark Pritchard has said the Juno-106 played bass and some of the pads, which they pitch-shifted with a Zoom unit, and that the signature reverb was an Alesis Quadraverb on a chorus-reverb setting: noisy and detuned.

jupiter-6.on: Roland Jupiter-6 layered with an Oberheim Matrix-1000
jupiter-6.text: For the remix, not the album version, Steve Rodway added a lead hook with a little portamento, layering a Jupiter-6 with a Matrix-1000.

jupiter-8.text: The bubbling riff is the Jupiter-8’s arpeggiator, run with a sequencer and a TR-808 drum machine. The backing track was built in a day.
Nick Rhodes’ Jupiter-8 plays the arpeggiated figure that opens the song.

jupiter-8.on: Roland Jupiter-8, with a Roland TR-808 drum machine
jupiter-8.text: The held synth pad the whole track is built on is a Jupiter-8, over a TR-808 pattern. Gaye’s guitarist Gordon Banks has said those two machines were the only electronic instruments used.

Johannes Schmoelling played the hypnotic line on the Jupiter-8’s arpeggiator rather than a sequencer, set to random instead of up or down. Two Jupiter-8s were synced together, panned apart and sent through a delay timed to the pattern.

jupiter-8.on: Roland Jupiter-8 sequenced from a Roland MC-4, with a Fairlight CMI and a LinnDrum
jupiter-8.text: Session player Andy Richards’ Jupiter-8, driven by an MC-4 sequencer, plays chords and the sound effects, including the explosion near the end. Producer Trevor Horn described them as “Andy playing his JP8”.
Jonathan Cain has said the opening synth riff is a Jupiter-8.
The Jupiter-8 was at the centre of Howard Jones’ one-man live and studio set-up for his first album.
The theme from Beverly Hills Cop. The sawtooth lead is a Jupiter-8; the bass is a Moog modular and the drums a LinnDrum.

jupiter-8.on: Roland Jupiter-8 (arpeggio and pads), with a LinnDrum
jupiter-8.text: The Jupiter-8’s arpeggiator runs through almost every section except the chorus, with sawtooth pads from the same synth on top.
Hammer said he used the Jupiter-8 for the rolling bass line. The single reached number two in the UK.

jupiter-8.on: Roland Jupiter-8 (the lead), with an Oberheim, a Sequential Pro-One and a Roland SH-2
jupiter-8.text: The theme’s arpeggio is played on an Oberheim Two Voice, by hand rather than by a sequencer.

k2.text: Clarke is a long-standing MS-20 owner and has used it for basses and effects across decades of records.

k2.on: Roland SH-101 and Korg MS-20, among other home-modified gear
k2.text: Richard D. James has named the MS-20 among the handful of cheap instruments the early records were made on, and its screaming resonant filter runs through them.
The duo have listed the MS-20 among the second-hand analogue gear the first album was built on, at a time when the instrument was still cheap.
Both play the MS-20 on the album; Godin is credited with it on “Sexy Boy”, and Dunckel plays the intro of “All I Need” on it.
The lead line that carried the record is probably the best-known MS-20 part ever put on tape.
Will Gregory’s buzzing glam bass and lead sounds.
Damian Taylor, who worked on the album, has said most of the synth lines on the track are the MS-20 put through a lot of distortion and fuzz.
The squiggling synth lines that run through the track come from the MS-20, usually with effects on top.

k2.on: Korg MS-20 and Roland SH-2 (the bass riffs)
k2.text: Daniel Hunt said most of the bass riffs are an SH-2 or an MS-20, and that the effects they were put through mattered as much as the synths: some parts listeners take for guitar are synths, and the other way round.
The band’s return leaned on old analogue monosynths for its harsher textures, the MS-20 among them.
Hopkins has said every synth sound in the track is the MS-20, which is unusual — most records use it for one part.
The MS-20 runs through the album, including the title track. Yorke has used one in his own work for years, though it is not documented on Radiohead’s own records.
Meaker built the drums from other sources, but all the bass and synth sounds on the track are the MS-20. Whether it is an original or one of Korg’s reissues is not stated.

kobol.text: The Kobol is listed among the album’s instruments, and the sleeve thanks RSF.

kobol.who: Depeche Mode, with producer Daniel Miller
kobol.text: Miller told Electronics & Music Maker that the band used “an RSF expander module” in the studio alongside the PPG, and praised its voltage control of every setting and the speed of its envelopes. He did not name the tracks it was used on.

kobol.who: Jean-Michel Jarre, with Frédérick Rousseau and Dominique Perrier
kobol.text: For the 1981 concerts in China, Rousseau played sequences and bass lines on a rack of Kobol Expanders driven by an MDB Polysequencer.

model-15.on: Moog Grandmother, with a Moog Matriarch and a Prophet
model-15.text: Tygner played the album’s synth parts by hand and ran them through a Vermona RetroVerb for spring reverb and a little drive. Which tracks use the Grandmother is not stated.

model-d.text: Every line played and overdubbed separately. The record that made "Moog" a household word.
George Harrison’s modular, used for ribbon-like lead lines and white-noise wind.
Keith Emerson’s closing solo: a square-wave lead with heavy glide, improvised in one take.
Moog lent Sun Ra a prototype before the Model D went on sale. He used it for noise, clusters and free solos.

model-d.on: Moog modular, over Hammond organ and piano
model-d.text: Keith Emerson overdubbed Moog parts on the title suite; “Aquatarkus” has a long Moog solo.

model-d.what: Close to the Edge, The Six Wives of Henry VIII
model-d.text: Fast, bright sawtooth solos played against Hammond and Mellotron. Wakeman toured with several Minimoogs so he did not have to re-set one between songs.
Four long pieces, one for each season, that mix slow Moog sounds with recordings of wind, rain, birds and insects. An early example of what was later called ambient music.

Hammer took up the Minimoog for the band’s second album. On “One Word” he takes the third solo after John McLaughlin’s guitar and Jerry Goodman’s violin, bending notes with the pitch wheel as a guitarist would.
The bass line that runs through the whole piece.
A squelching, resonant bass played by hand, with the filter doing the talking.

model-d.on: Moog III modular, with a Mellotron
model-d.text: Debussy’s piano pieces, including “Clair de Lune” and “Arabesque No. 1”, arranged and overdubbed voice by voice on the Moog. It was nominated for four Grammy Awards.
Richard Wright’s horn-like lead over the opening pad.

model-d.on: A small Moog modular, a Minimoog and an Oberheim SEM, with sequencers
model-d.text: Rock arrangements in which every part is a synthesizer, multitracked by Fast alone. It sold more than any all-electronic album since Switched-On Bach.

model-d.on: Minimoog, with ARP Pro Soloist and ARP String Ensemble
model-d.text: Bernie Worrell is credited with Minimoog among his keyboards. His gliding, warbling synth lines run through the title track, “Mothership Connection (Star Child)”.
Christopher Franke’s Moog modular plays the plucked bass sequence of Part I from its 960 sequencers, with Mellotron, organ and other synths over it.
Manfred Mann played his leads on a Minimoog: a singing, resonant line with vibrato brought in by hand on the long notes.

model-d.on: Minimoog, ARP Odyssey, Micromoog, Polymoog and a Moog 15 modular
model-d.text: Corea is credited with five synthesizers alongside piano, Rhodes, Clavinet and organ. Which one plays each part is not set out track by track.

Hammer plays synthesizer on “Led Boots”, “Come Dancing”, “Blue Wind” and “Play with Me”, trading bent, guitar-like lines with Beck. On “Blue Wind”, which he wrote and produced, he also plays drums and keyboard bass.
Bernie Worrell played the bass line on Minimoog rather than bass guitar, and funk bass changed with it.
The pulsing sequencer bass that pointed the way to disco, Hi-NRG and techno.

model-d.on: Minimoog (the bass lines), with a Roland SH-2000 for the melody
model-d.text: The director Alan Parker asked for something in the manner of “I Feel Love”. The pulsing bass lines are a Minimoog and the melody a Roland SH-2000; Harold Faltermeyer arranged the music under Moroder.
Numan found a Minimoog left in the studio and rebuilt his band’s sound around it: a buzzing lead and an open, droning bass.

model-d.on: Minimoog and Sequential Circuits Prophet-5, with an ARP Solina string ensemble
model-d.text: Geoff Downes made the overdubbed orchestral parts from a Solina, a Minimoog and a Prophet-5. Its video was the first one MTV showed when the channel opened in 1981.

model-d.on: Minimoog, with Roger Troutman’s talk box
model-d.text: Roger Troutman sang through an Electro-Harmonix “Golden Throat” talk box driven by a Minimoog, and the bass line is usually credited to a Minimoog too. Produced by Bootsy Collins and Troutman, it reached number two on the US soul chart.

model-d.on: Minimoog (the bass), with an Elka string synthesizer and a Roland CR-78 drum machine
model-d.text: Warren Cann’s CR-78 pattern was the starting point. Under the piano, viola and Midge Ure’s voice, the slow bass line is a Minimoog. Released as a single in 1981, it reached number two in the UK.
On “Egypt” Max Middleton plays a Minimoog and Michael Moran a Prophet-5, according to the album credits.

model-d.on: Minimoog, with a Korg miniKORG 700 and a Korg 800DV
model-d.text: Music for the NHK television series about the Silk Road, composed mainly on these three synthesizers. Kitaro named the same three as his favourites in 1989, and said a Minimoog fitted with MIDI did not sound the same as an unmodified one.

model-d.on: Two ARP Odysseys, a Yamaha CS-80 and a Minimoog, with a Fairlight CMI on “Fade to Grey”
model-d.text: Rusty Egan listed the synths in 1984: two Odysseys, a CS-80, a Minimoog and several Yamaha string machines, shared by Billy Currie and Dave Formula. The producer Richard James Burgess programmed a Fairlight that was used heavily on “Fade to Grey”. Which synth plays each part is not documented.
Geddy Lee played the lead on a Minimoog, and told Keyboard magazine in 1984 that he did not think he would do that again.

model-d.on: Moog Source, played by Matthew Seligman
model-d.text: The bass line, a piccolo-trumpet line and the falling “phone” part after the chorus are a Moog Source, played by Dolby’s bass guitarist.
The bass line is two Minimoogs layered.
The octave-jumping sequenced bass.
The high, gliding sine-like lead that became the signature of G-funk.

model-d.on: Minimoog, Sequential Circuits Prophet VS and Oberheim OB-Mx, with Akai samplers
model-d.text: Reznor’s equipment for the album included a Minimoog, a Prophet VS and an Oberheim OB-Mx alongside samplers and guitars. Which part each synth plays is not documented track by track.

The album credits list Nicolas Godin on Minimoog on five tracks and Jean-Benoît Dunckel on Minimoog on “Kelly Watch the Stars” and “Talisman”, with Moog solos on “La Femme d’argent”, “Sexy Boy” and others.
Round, sliding sub bass played by hand. His custom Voyager is now in the Smithsonian.

neutron.text: Winter hung the 2600’s keyboard round his neck and played filter sweeps and sample-and-hold runs as a lead instrument.
The bass line: a synth doing the job of the bass guitar on a hit jazz-funk record.
An eight-note sequence sped up, with the filter and noise worked by hand.
Zawinul played two 2600s, one with its keyboard scaled upside down so that familiar fingerings gave unfamiliar lines.

neutron.what: Star Wars — the voice of R2-D2
neutron.text: Patched whistles and chirps mixed with Burtt’s own voice.
Producer Daniel Miller made the kick and snare sounds on a 2600 with a sequencer in place of a drum machine: a pitch-swept sine for the kick, filtered noise for the snare.

neutron.on: Roland SH-101 and Korg MS-20, among other home-modified gear
neutron.text: Simple 3340-style mono lines, delay and a great deal of modulation.

neutron.what: Music Has the Right to Children
neutron.text: Detuned, slowly wavering leads made to sound like worn tape.
A distorted, rubbery bass line made on one small semi-modular.
Will Gregory’s buzzing glam bass and lead sounds.
Every element of the drum and bass track was made on one Neutron, an idea that began as a demonstration video for Behringer. It was released on Symmetry Recordings.

poly-d.text: Not a Poly D record: the bass line was played on the Minimoog whose panel the Poly D copies.

poly-d.on: Minimoog, with ARP Pro Soloist and ARP String Ensemble
poly-d.text: Not a Poly D record: Bernie Worrell played these lines on the Minimoog whose panel the Poly D copies.
Not a Poly D record: Bernie Worrell played the bass line on a Minimoog rather than a bass guitar.
Not a Poly D record: a buzzing Minimoog lead and a droning bass at the centre of the band’s sound.
The Poly D is listed as used on the album. Which tracks and sounds it plays is not documented.

poly-d.what: BRIT Awards Rising Star session, Abbey Road
poly-d.text: Her keyboard player used a Poly D for the live session.
Kartell told MusicRadar the Poly D was one of the first hardware synths he bought while making the album, that it is the piece of gear he uses most, and that he uses it for basses and leads.
Kevin Ratajczak plays a Poly D in the video. Whether it is on the recording itself is not documented.

pro-1.text: Greg Hawkes’s hard-sync lead. The same sync switch is on this panel.
After two albums built on Moogs, Numan added a Prophet-5 for smoother, layered parts.
The dark, held chords under the drum machine.
Pulsing eighth-note bass and simple lead lines, recorded quickly to picture.
Richard Barbieri used Oscillator B to modulate pitch and filter for atonal, metallic tones that barely sound like a keyboard.
Clarke built most of the album from a Pro-One and a sequencer: riffs, bass and much of the percussion, each sound recorded as its own track.
The swooping synth parts that answer the vocal.

pro-1.on: Sequential Circuits Pro-One (bass line), sequenced from a drum machine
pro-1.text: The bass line is a Pro-One step sequence triggered by a drum machine. Juan Atkins has said he tried about three different note sequences before settling on a four-note pattern.

pro-1.on: Sequential Circuits Prophet-5, with piano, a Fairlight CMI and a LinnDrum
pro-1.text: Sakamoto’s first film score, for Nagisa Oshima’s film in which he also acted. The Prophet-5, which he named in interviews as his favourite synthesizer, plays most of the string-like parts.
Part of the one-man live rig he played early in his career, used for bass lines and solo lines.

pro-1.on: Sequential Circuits Pro-One (stabs and drones), through a Lexicon PCM60 reverb
pro-1.text: The stabs and drone effects are a Pro-One run through reverb. It was the first release on Atkins’s own label, Metroplex, recorded in his mother’s basement.
The soft electric-piano-like chords that open Kid A.

pro-1.on: Sequential Circuits Pro-One, Prophet-600 and Korg Polysix
pro-1.text: Moore has said these three synths are on every Zombi recording and go on every tour. On stage he uses the chord memory of the Prophet-600 and Polysix to play chords from one key while also covering the bass.

pro-1.on: Sequential Circuits Pro-One and Roland Juno-106
pro-1.text: Kevin Parker made the album’s synth parts mainly on these two, layered with guitars and warped audio.

pro-1.on: Sequential Circuits Pro-One, among his analogue synths
pro-1.text: Moore said in 2014, just after finishing the score, that his Pro-One had been used on every recording he had made since buying it in 2002, and that he uses it and his Prophet-600 on almost every score for atmospheres and Carpenter-style stings.

pro-1.on: Roland Juno-106 and Sequential Circuits Pro-One
pro-1.text: Parker kept the two synths he had used on Lonerism.

pro-1.on: Roland Jupiter-8 (the lead), with an Oberheim, a Sequential Pro-One and a Roland SH-2
pro-1.text: The theme’s arpeggio is played on an Oberheim Two Voice, by hand rather than by a sequencer.
Owens’s cover of Radiohead’s “Weird Fishes/Arpeggi” was worked out over MIDI on a Pro-One in two afternoons, a year before the rest of the album.

pro-800.text: Greg Hawkes played a Prophet-5 on Candy-O. The oscillator-sync lead of the kind heard on the band’s records is exactly what the PRO-800’s SYNC switch and Poly-Mod FIL ENV do.
The dark, slow chords that open the song were played on a Prophet-5.
Carpenter and Alan Howarth built the score on a Prophet-5: pulsing bass lines and slow, dark pads.

pro-800.on: Sequential Circuits Prophet-5, with piano, a Fairlight CMI and a LinnDrum
pro-800.text: Sakamoto’s first film score, for Nagisa Oshima’s film in which he also acted. The Prophet-5, which he named in interviews as his favourite synthesizer, plays most of the string-like parts.
Bernie Worrell plays the synth parts in the concert film, recorded at the Pantages Theatre in Hollywood in 1983. He has said he used Prophet-5s for his work with the band.

pro-800.on: Sequential Circuits Prophet-600, with an Alesis MMT-8 sequencer
pro-800.text: Carl Craig has said that when he started making music he had a Prophet-600, an MMT-8 sequencer and a four-track. His records of 1989–90 as Psyche and BFC were later collected on Elements 1989–1990; which tracks use the Prophet is not stated.

pro-800.on: Sequential Circuits Pro-One, Prophet-600 and Korg Polysix
pro-800.text: Moore has said these three synths are on every Zombi recording and go on every tour. On stage he uses the chord memory of the Prophet-600 and Polysix to play chords from one key while also covering the bass.

pro-800.on: Sequential Circuits Prophet-600, layered with bass guitar through effects pedals
pro-800.text: The album’s bass sounds were made by layering a Prophet-600 with bass guitar through a chain of effects pedals.

system-15.on: Moog modular, programmed by Paul Beaver
system-15.text: Micky Dolenz plays the swooping, whistling fills on his own Moog, one of the first three sold.

system-15.on: Moog modular, set up by Paul Beaver
system-15.text: Jim Morrison’s vocal was fed through the Moog so that it could be played from the keyboard, giving the voice its wavering, processed sound. One of the earliest uses of the Moog on a rock record.

system-15.on: Moog modular, with Ondioline and tape effects
system-15.text: The duo’s second album added the Moog to their tape loops and Ondioline, a year before Switched-On Bach. It was reissued in 1971 as Spotlight on the Moog.

system-15.on: Moog modular
system-15.text: Every line played and overdubbed separately. The record that made "Moog" a household word.

system-15.what: The Nonesuch Guide to Electronic Music
system-15.on: Moog III modular
system-15.text: A double album that goes through the Moog’s oscillators, filters, envelopes and noise one at a time, with a short piece, “Peace Three”, to close.

system-15.on: Moog modular
system-15.text: George Harrison’s modular, used for ribbon-like lead lines and white-noise wind.

system-15.on: Moog modular
system-15.text: Keith Emerson’s closing solo: a square-wave lead with heavy glide, improvised in one take.

system-15.on: Moog III modular
system-15.text: Florian Fricke’s Moog plays long held tones and slowly wandering lines over hand percussion: one of the first German records built around a synthesizer.

system-15.on: Moog modular, with a vocoder built by Robert Moog
system-15.text: Carlos’s Moog versions of Beethoven and Purcell and her own “Timesteps”. The sung parts of the Ninth Symphony and of “Timesteps” were put through the vocoder.

system-15.on: Moog modular, over Hammond organ and piano
system-15.text: Keith Emerson overdubbed Moog parts on the title suite; “Aquatarkus” has a long Moog solo.

system-15.on: TONTO, built around a Moog III modular
system-15.text: Every sound on the album comes from Cecil and Margouleff’s expanded Moog system. Stevie Wonder heard it and asked to work with them.

system-15.on: Moog synthesizer (the TONTO system), under a Hohner Clavinet riff
system-15.text: Wonder is credited with Moog bass; Malcolm Cecil and Robert Margouleff programmed the sound on TONTO. The riff on top is a Clavinet, not a synth.

system-15.on: Moog modular, with field recordings
system-15.text: Four long pieces, one for each season, that mix slow Moog sounds with recordings of wind, rain, birds and insects. An early example of what was later called ambient music.

system-15.on: Moog modular (the TONTO system)
system-15.text: A squelching, resonant bass played by hand, with the filter doing the talking.

system-15.on: Moog modular with its sequencer
system-15.text: Christopher Franke’s Moog modular and its sequencer play the repeating bass patterns that the band shifted and filtered by hand, live in the studio: the start of the Berlin-school sequencer sound.

system-15.on: Moog III modular, with a Mellotron
system-15.text: Debussy’s piano pieces, including “Clair de Lune” and “Arabesque No. 1”, arranged and overdubbed voice by voice on the Moog. It was nominated for four Grammy Awards.

system-15.on: A small Moog modular, a Minimoog and an Oberheim SEM, with sequencers
system-15.text: Rock arrangements in which every part is a synthesizer, multitracked by Fast alone. It sold more than any all-electronic album since Switched-On Bach.

system-15.on: Moog modular with 960 sequencers
system-15.text: Christopher Franke’s Moog modular plays the plucked bass sequence of Part I from its 960 sequencers, with Mellotron, organ and other synths over it.

system-15.on: Moog modular (Florian Fricke’s Moog IIIp and sequencer cabinet)
system-15.text: Schulze’s first album on the large Moog he bought from Florian Fricke of Popol Vuh late in 1975, used within weeks of buying it.

system-15.on: Moog modular
system-15.text: Short, melodic pieces written for houseplants to listen to, all played on the Moog. It was first given away by a Los Angeles plant shop and with mattresses sold at Sears.

system-15.on: Minimoog, ARP Odyssey, Micromoog, Polymoog and a Moog 15 modular
system-15.text: Corea is credited with five synthesizers alongside piano, Rhodes, Clavinet and organ. Which one plays each part is not set out track by track.

system-15.on: Moog modular with sequencer
system-15.text: The pulsing sequencer bass that pointed the way to disco, Hi-NRG and techno.

system-15.on: Moog Series III modular, patched by Dan Wyman, with piano
system-15.text: Carpenter played most of the parts while Dan Wyman, a music professor at San Jose State University, set up the patches on his expanded Moog modular and joined in on the hardest lines. The score was recorded at Sound Arts in Los Angeles.

system-15.on: Moog III-C with a Roland MC-8 Microcomposer, with an Oberheim Eight Voice, a Polymoog, a Minimoog, an ARP Odyssey and a Korg PS-3100
system-15.text: Sakamoto’s first solo album, made just before Yellow Magic Orchestra formed. He played and programmed the synthesizers himself, with Hideki Matsutake operating the MC-8 computer sequencer that drove the Moog III-C.

system-15.on: Moog III-C modular driven by a Roland MC-8 Microcomposer, with a Minimoog, a Polymoog, ARP Odysseys and a Korg PS-3100
system-15.text: Hideki Matsutake typed the parts into the MC-8, which played the Moog modular and the other synths. He gave the machine-played lines their swing by making small changes to the timing he entered.

tb-303.what: Synthesizing: Ten Ragas to a Disco Beat
tb-303.text: An Indian film musician’s album of ragas played on a TB-303, TR-808 and Jupiter-8. Rediscovered decades later for sounding like acid house five years early.

tb-303.who: Sleezy D (Derrick Harris), produced by Marshall Jefferson
tb-303.on: Roland TB-303, with a Roland TR-808
tb-303.text: Released on Trax in 1986, a year before “Acid Tracks”, with a TB-303 line under Sleezy D’s voice. Marshall Jefferson has said he did not know how to programme the 303 and just hit some notes.
DJ Pierre, Spanky and Herb J’s long track built on a TB-303 pattern whose filter and resonance are moved by hand throughout.

tb-303.on: Roland TB-303, with a Roland TR-707
tb-303.text: A loose, overdriven TB-303 line over a heavily swung TR-707 pattern, made when Armando was seventeen.
A TB-303 plays a counter-riff, which Simpson has said also covered up timing problems between the machines.

tb-303.who: 808 State (Graham Massey, Martin Price, Gerald Simpson)
tb-303.text: Graham Massey has said the 303 was central to the album, which was recorded over a weekend at Spirit Studios in Manchester in January 1988.

tb-303.on: Roland TB-303, with a Yamaha DX100 bass line
tb-303.text: Paul Hartnoll made the track at home before going to the pub, recording it live onto cassette. A 303 runs under the sampled chime refrain, with a big DX100 bass line and a TR-909.
German acid techno built from several TB-303s at once, with long filter builds.

tb-303.on: Roland TB-303, with a Roland TR-606
tb-303.text: Richie Hawtin has said the album came together when he paired the TR-606 with the TB-303, the drum machine it was designed to partner, and jammed live on the two for most of 48 hours.
A long, hypnotic acid techno track built on a single repeating 303 line.
The main line is a TB-303 played through distortion, in a slow, funky groove rather than an acid squelch.
A 303 line that builds for most of the track, its resonance and cutoff pushed until it screams.

tb-303.on: Roland TB-303, sampled and played back at half speed
tb-303.text: The album version adds a 303 line that is not on the 1992 single. Played back at half speed, every slide, accent and delay can be heard, alongside samples of the Bulgarian singer Yanka Rupkina.
A sample-built big-beat track whose TB-303 line comes out of the breakdown, filtered at first and then opened up into a squelch.

tb-303.on: Roland SH-101 and TB-303, with a Synton Fenix modular and a Roland MC-4 sequencer
tb-303.text: A series of eleven vinyl EPs made mostly on analogue synths, drum machines and sequencers, after years of computer-based records.

Acid techno built from several 303 lines rolling at once.

A TB-303 played through distortion, the job the TD-3’s built-in distortion does.
A screaming, heavily driven 303 line that builds for most of the track.

ub-xa-d.text: Geddy Lee developed the melody from improvisations he played on the OB-X at soundchecks. The growling sweep is the OB-X with its voices stacked on one note; small differences between the voices’ filters and envelopes keep the sound shifting.
The OB-Xa is at the centre of the early-80s Minneapolis sound: short, bright synth stabs playing the parts a horn section would have played.

ub-xa-d.on: Oberheim OB-Xa, with a Linn LM-1
ub-xa-d.text: Prince played the OB-Xa and programmed the LM-1 himself. The song builds from the drum machine and slow synth chords into a rock chorus.
Eddie Van Halen wrote the song on an OB-Xa, and its chord riff is the best-known Oberheim brass sound. The synth solo in the middle is the OB-Xa too.

ub-xa-d.on: Oberheim OB-Xa and Yamaha DX7, with a Linn LM-1
ub-xa-d.text: Prince recorded the fast, baroque-sounding synth line at half speed and an octave lower, then played the tape back at normal speed. Matt Fink said this gave the part its staccato, classical feel.

The first single with Sammy Hagar singing, it began as a jam in which Eddie Van Halen played the riff on an OB-8. Hagar said the riff sounded like a guitar part, where “Jump” had sounded like a synthesizer. On tour Van Halen played it from a keyboard on stage linked by MIDI to an OB-8 kept backstage.
Producer Jim Abbiss stripped the song back to a four-to-the-floor beat and built it up again from an OB-Xa drone. The OB-Xa and a Korg Mono/Poly were the only keyboards on the album.
